title: Latency-slot reservation: attention-cost guided prefill/decode split
creator: Aisha Malik
description:
Background: As load grows we observe tail latency regressions for low-latency customers caused by long-attention prefill requests occupying shared prefill/decode slots. Current phase-splitting heuristics prioritize token-count and age but do not account for attention-operator cost (seq_len^2 hotspots, sparse attention variants). This ticket proposes a slot-reservation and admission policy that uses an attention-cost signal to split work into fast-path slots (latency reserved) and best-effort slots (throughput), reducing p95/p99 regressions while preserving overall throughput.

Proposal: 1) Add an 'attention_cost' scalar estimated at prefill admission time computed from batch statistics (max seq_len, avg seq_len, attention_type, model_arch tags). 2) Maintain two slot pools per-GPU: latency_slots (small fixed count) and throughput_slots (elastic). 3) Admission rules: if attention_cost <= latency_threshold and request has low-latency tag -> attempt latency_slot; otherwise go to throughput queue. 4) Opportunistic consolidation: small high-attention prefill requests can be split into micro-phases and co-scheduled with decode if consolidation reduces total attention work on latency slots. 5) Fallbacks: if latency_slots are saturated for > latency_saturation_window, allow low-attention requests to spill into throughput_slots with best-effort hedging.

Key trade-offs: - Conserving latency slots improves SLOs for critical customers but may slightly reduce aggregate GPU utilization. - Estimating attention cost must be conservative to avoid misclassification. - Micro-phase splitting introduces additional context-switch overhead and KV cache management complexity.

Implementation plan (API/runtime changes): - Prefill admission hook returns attention_cost and recommended_slot. - Scheduler: add slot pool accounting, token-budget eviction rules, and micro-phase splitter that yields temporary KV checkpointing. - Metrics: slot occupancy, starvations, p50/p95/p99 latency by customer tier, GPU utilization, cost-per-token.

Acceptance criteria: - Experiment A: traffic tagged as low-latency shows p95 reduction >= 30% and p99 reduction >= 25% vs baseline under mixed load. - Overall token throughput across cluster within 5% of baseline after 24h steady-state. - No increase in request error rate > 0.1%. - Starvation count for non-latency traffic limited per-sla (configurable).

Test plan: - Unit tests for attention_cost estimator with synthetic seq_len distributions. - Integration test that simulates mixed workload (tail-heavy long-prefill and high-throughput short requests) using local simulator harness. - Staging experiment with 10% of production traffic, A/B against current scheduler, monitor metrics in runtime-ops dashboard and set automated rollback if p99 for any customer tier regresses > 10%.
acceptance_criteria: 1) p95_latency_reduction_for_low_latency_tag >= 30% over baseline under mixed load; 2) p99_latency_reduction_for_low_latency_tag >= 25%; 3) cluster_throughput_drop <= 5% after 24h; 4) error_rate_increase <= 0.1%; 5) starvation_count configurable and within target
rollout_plan: Phase 0: feature flag behind runtime.experimental.attn_slot (dev only). Phase 1: internal canary on dedicated/staging clusters with synthetic traffic (1 day). Phase 2: 10% traffic via A/B for select low-latency customers (48h). Phase 3: 50% traffic (1 week) with autoscaling thresholds tuned. Phase 4: full rollout with backfill to convert throughput-only long-prefill patterns into best-effort batches.
risks:
- Mis-estimation of attention_cost leading to mis-routing and wasted latency slots.
- Micro-phase splitting may increase KV checkpoint churn and memory pressure.
- Unexpected interactions with existing batching/caching heuristics causing regression in long-tail throughput.
- Complexity increases operational burden and debugging surface for incidents.
